## Overview

`revlitquery` performs a **reverse literature search**: you give it a handful of
papers you already know are relevant (the *seed corpus*), and it reverse-engineers
a boolean query for **PubMed** and **Google Scholar** (at most 256 characters)
that finds those papers and as few irrelevant ones as possible.

Nothing about the topic is hardcoded. Concepts, synonyms, wildcards and
exclusions are all discovered from the text of the seed papers and of the
non-seed papers a draft query returns.

The figure below summarises the eight steps. The rest of this vignette explains
each one and runs a small, fully offline example on a synthetic corpus (no
network access needed).

```{r diagram, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7.4, fig.height = 5.4, fig.alt = "Flow diagram of the eight steps of the revlitquery workflow, from BibTeX seed parsing to the Pareto frontier of PubMed and Google Scholar queries."}
steps <- data.frame(
  id    = 1:8,
  title = c("Parse seeds", "Enrich with PubMed", "Extract terms",
            "Discover concepts", "Build candidates",
            "Mine exclusions", "Refine neighbours", "Pareto frontier"),
  fn    = c("parse_bibtex()", "enrich_seeds()", "extract_candidate_terms()",
            "build_concept_blocks()", "generate_initial_candidates()",
            "discover_exclusion_hints()", "optimize_queries()",
            "write_optimization_report()"),
  what  = c("BibTeX file\n-> seed table", "PMIDs, abstracts,\nMeSH, keywords",
            "n-grams, wildcards,\nPubMed lift", "graph clusters ->\nAND / OR blocks",
            "block tiers x fields\n(<= 256 chars)", "noise topics ->\nNOT terms",
            "add / drop / swap\nterms and fields", "recall vs. hits,\nPubMed + Scholar"),
  stage = c("Input", "Input", "Discovery", "Discovery",
            "Optimization", "Optimization", "Optimization", "Output"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
# Snake layout: steps 1-4 left-to-right on the top row, 5-8 right-to-left below
sp <- 1.35
steps$x <- sp * c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1)
steps$y <- c(2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1)
bw <- 0.60; bh <- 0.36

arrows <- data.frame(
  x    = c(1 * sp + bw, 2 * sp + bw, 3 * sp + bw, 4 * sp, 4 * sp - bw, 3 * sp - bw, 2 * sp - bw),
  y    = c(2, 2, 2, 2 - bh, 1, 1, 1),
  xend = c(2 * sp - bw, 3 * sp - bw, 4 * sp - bw, 4 * sp, 3 * sp + bw, 2 * sp + bw, 1 * sp + bw),
  yend = c(2, 2, 2, 1 + bh, 1, 1, 1)
)

steps$stage <- factor(steps$stage, levels = c("Input", "Discovery", "Optimization", "Output"))
stage_cols <- c(Input = "#8da0cb", Discovery = "#66c2a5",
                Optimization = "#fc8d62", Output = "#e78ac3")

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = arrows, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.16, "cm"), type = "closed"),
    linewidth = 0.7, colour = "grey35"
  ) +
  geom_rect(
    data = steps,
    aes(xmin = x - bw, xmax = x + bw, ymin = y - bh, ymax = y + bh, fill = stage),
    colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_text(data = steps, aes(x = x - bw + 0.05, y = y + bh - 0.07,
                              label = id), hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
            fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  geom_text(data = steps, aes(x = x, y = y + 0.09, label = title),
            fontface = "bold", size = 3.3) +
  geom_text(data = steps, aes(x = x, y = y - 0.06, label = fn),
            family = "mono", size = 2.1, colour = "grey15") +
  geom_text(data = steps, aes(x = x, y = y - 0.19, label = what),
            size = 2.5, lineheight = 0.9, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = stage_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.65, 6.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.55, 2.5)) +
  labs(
    title = "revlitquery workflow",
    subtitle = "Seed papers in, Pareto-optimal PubMed and Google Scholar queries out"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30"),
    plot.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6)
  )
```

The whole pipeline is wrapped by `optimize_search_queries()`; every step is also
exported so you can run, inspect, or replace it individually.

## A synthetic seed corpus

To keep the example offline, we build the seed table by hand. In real use,
steps 1 and 2 produce exactly this structure from your BibTeX file.

```{r seeds}
titles <- c(
  "Pollinator decline in fragmented agricultural landscapes",
  "Wild bee pollinator richness decline across fragmented farmland",
  "Bumblebee abundance loss in fragmented agricultural habitats",
  "Pollinator diversity loss in fragmented agroecosystem landscapes",
  "Solitary bee decline across fragmented cropland habitats",
  "Pollinator richness loss in fragmented agricultural ecosystems",
  "Pesticide exposure drives pollinator decline in farmland",
  "Hoverfly pollinator abundance decline in fragmented meadows"
)
seeds <- tibble::tibble(
  seed_id = seq_along(titles),
  citekey = paste0("seed", seq_along(titles)),
  year = as.character(2016 + seq_along(titles)),
  doi = "",
  pmid = as.character(1000 + seq_along(titles)),
  in_pubmed = TRUE,
  full_title = titles,
  full_abstract = titles,
  full_text = titles,
  mesh_terms = rep(list(character(0)), length(titles)),
  all_keywords = rep(list(character(0)), length(titles))
)
seeds[, c("citekey", "full_title")]
```

## Step 1: Parse the seed BibTeX file

`parse_bibtex()` reads a `.bib` file, cleans LaTeX markup, and extracts titles,
abstracts, DOIs, PMIDs and keywords. It tolerates concatenated strings,
nested braces and malformed entries.

```r
seeds_raw <- parse_bibtex("path/to/seed_articles.bib")
```

## Step 2: Enrich seeds with PubMed

`enrich_seeds()` resolves each reference to a PubMed record by PMID, then DOI,
then fuzzy title match (`title_jaccard()`). It adds PubMed abstracts, MeSH
headings and author keywords, and flags seeds that are not in PubMed
(`in_pubmed = FALSE`). Calls follow the NCBI usage policy (identified tool name,
HTTP POST, rate limiting) and are cached on disk.

```r
seeds <- enrich_seeds(seeds_raw, cache_dir = ".cache")
```

## Step 3: Extract and score candidate terms

`extract_candidate_terms()` mines 1- to 3-grams from titles and abstracts and
**synthesizes prefix wildcards** (for example `decreas*`, `pollinat*`) when
several corpus words share a stem that rescues extra seeds. A multi-layer
set-cover shortlist keeps terms from several independent facets of the corpus,
plus rare terms that rescue outlier papers. Each shortlisted term is probed in
PubMed for its background frequency, giving a **lift** (how over-represented the
term is in your seeds compared to PubMed overall).

Here a function replaces the live PubMed probe:

```{r terms}
fake_bg <- function(term) {
  switch(term,
    "pollinator" = 9000L, "decline" = 120000L, "fragmented" = 15000L,
    40000L
  )
}
terms <- extract_candidate_terms(seeds, probe_pubmed = TRUE, eval_bg_fn = fake_bg)
head(terms[, c("term", "df_tiab", "bg_hits", "lift")], 8)
```

## Step 4: Discover concept blocks

Instead of a predefined concept list, `build_concept_blocks()` discovers the
structure of the topic from the data:

1. The best high-lift anchor becomes the **primary topic** block.
2. `discover_term_clusters()` builds a graph of candidate terms. Edges combine
   local-context and MeSH/keyword similarity (a small latent semantic analysis),
   coverage complementarity (two terms that cover different seeds are likely
   interchangeable `OR` synonyms), and lexical similarity. Louvain community
   detection then groups terms into concepts.
3. Within each community a greedy set-cover grows an `OR` block; blocks are
   combined with `AND`.

```{r blocks}
blocks <- build_concept_blocks(
  terms, seeds,
  max_blocks = 3L,
  probe_selectivity = TRUE,
  eval_joint_fn = function(t1, t2) 2500L   # stand-in for a PubMed joint count
)
for (b in blocks) cat(sprintf("%-22s %s\n", b$name, paste(b$terms, collapse = " | ")))
```

You can always override discovery with `custom_blocks` in the configuration.

## Step 5: Build and translate candidate queries

`generate_initial_candidates()` combines block specificity tiers and fields
(title vs. title/abstract) into diverse candidates, discarding any that exceed
256 characters once translated. A query is a canonical object that
`to_pubmed_query()` and `to_google_scholar_query()` translate into each syntax
(Google Scholar has no truncation operator, so wildcards are expanded to the
dominant corpus word or a morphological stem).

```{r queries}
q <- make_query(list(
  list(name = "topic",   field = "tiab", terms = c("pollinat*", "bee")),
  list(name = "trend",   field = "tiab", terms = c("decline", "loss"))
), exclude_terms = "pesticide")

cat(to_pubmed_query(q), "\n")
cat(to_google_scholar_query(q), "\n")
gs_char_count(q)
```

Without network access, `estimate_local_query()` scores a query against the seed
texts, which is what the optimizer uses to pre-rank candidates before spending
PubMed calls.

```{r local}
est <- estimate_local_query(q, terms, seeds)
c(local_recall = est$local_recall, seeds_found = est$local_found)
```

## Step 6: Mine exclusion hints

`discover_exclusion_hints()` samples non-seed articles returned by the best
draft query and finds what makes them noise. Candidate `NOT` terms (words,
phrases, and synthesized wildcards) are checked locally against the seeds so
none that would drop a seed is recommended blindly. Terms are then partitioned
into **noise topics** by an NPMI/Jaccard co-occurrence graph with Louvain
clustering (`cluster_exclusion_terms()`), and a greedy set-cover builds
compact exclusion bundles that fit in the 256-character budget. Verified hit
reductions come from live PubMed counts.

```{r noise}
noise_terms <- c("xenograft", "mice", "vitro", "resection", "laparoscopic", "biopsy")
noise_cov <- list(
  c(rep(TRUE, 6), rep(FALSE, 6)), c(rep(TRUE, 5), rep(FALSE, 7)),
  c(FALSE, rep(TRUE, 5), rep(FALSE, 6)), c(rep(FALSE, 6), rep(TRUE, 6)),
  c(rep(FALSE, 6), rep(TRUE, 5), FALSE), c(rep(FALSE, 7), rep(TRUE, 5))
)
as.character(cluster_exclusion_terms(noise_terms, noise_cov))
```

## Step 7: Refine neighbours

`optimize_queries()` runs a two-stage search under a fixed evaluation budget
(`max_evals`). **Stage 1** evaluates the initial candidates live. **Stage 2a**
adds exclusion-refined variants. **Stage 2b** greedily generates neighbours of
the current Pareto queries: prune a term, switch a field, swap in a narrower
variant, add a rescue term from the same concept cluster for seeds still
missed, add a qualifier block, or extend the exclusions. Each round re-evaluates
the most promising neighbours and stops once the frontier stops improving.

## Step 8: Read the Pareto frontier

Every evaluated query has a recall (share of seeds found) and a hit count
(PubMed results). The **Pareto frontier** keeps queries that no other query beats
on both axes. `write_optimization_report()` exports it with PubMed and Google
Scholar strings and links; the Shiny app (`run_revlitquery_app()`) shows it
interactively.

```{r pareto}
frontier_demo <- data.frame(
  recall = c(0.62, 0.75, 0.88, 0.94, 1.00, 0.70, 0.90, 0.85),
  hits   = c(120, 210, 340, 430, 780, 400, 900, 600)
)
frontier_demo$is_pareto <- compute_pareto_frontier(
  data.frame(combined_recall = frontier_demo$recall, pm_hits = frontier_demo$hits,
             gs_chars = 100L, n_terms = 4L)
)
ggplot(frontier_demo, aes(hits, recall)) +
  geom_step(data = subset(frontier_demo, is_pareto), direction = "hv",
            colour = "#d95f02") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = is_pareto), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#d95f02", `FALSE` = "grey60"),
                      labels = c("Dominated", "Pareto-optimal"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "PubMed hits (lower is more precise)", y = "Seed recall",
       title = "Illustrative sensitivity-specificity frontier") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Pick the point on the frontier that matches your review: a high-recall query for
systematic reviews, or a compact query for quick scoping.

## Putting it together

All eight steps run in one call:

```r
res <- optimize_search_queries(
  bib_path   = "path/to/seed_articles.bib",
  output_dir = "output",
  min_recall = 0.90,
  max_hits   = 1000
)
res$pareto_df
```

See `vignette("cli-and-r-workflow")` for command-line options and
`vignette("shiny-interface")` for the interactive dashboard.
